title: SQL runtime: graded exercises (hr / shop / events)

blocks.md: Each exercise runs your SQL and the authored solution on **every** listed dataset (the second is a hidden `_edge` twin that breaks plausible wrong answers). Submit grades them all; the draft is saved as you type.

blocks.title: Departments with no employees
blocks.prompt: List the **name of every department that has no employees**. Return one column `dept_name`.
blocks.starter:
-- one row per empty department
SELECT d.dept_name
FROM departments d
WHERE 
ORDER BY d.dept_name;
hints: A LEFT JOIN from departments to employees puts NULLs on the employee side for empty departments.
`WHERE e.emp_id IS NULL` after a LEFT JOIN is the classic test. If you use NOT IN, remember what one NULL in the subquery does to the whole result.
NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe here: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id)`.

blocks.title: Top salary per department
blocks.prompt: For every `dept_id` that appears in `employees` (NULL included), return `dept_id` and the highest `salary` in it as `top_salary`, **ordered by `dept_id` ascending**. NULL salaries must not poison MAX.
blocks.solution:
SELECT e.dept_id,
       MAX(e.salary) AS top_salary
FROM employees e
GROUP BY e.dept_id
ORDER BY e.dept_id;
blocks.starter:
SELECT ,
       MAX(e.salary) AS top_salary
FROM employees e
GROUP BY

hints: GROUP BY the grouping column itself — NULL is its own group.
MAX ignores NULLs, so a NULL salary never wins the max.
ORDER BY dept_id ASC puts the NULL group last in PostgreSQL (NULLS LAST is the default for ASC).

blocks.title: Net paid per customer
blocks.prompt: Return `customer_id` and `total_paid` — the **net amount each customer paid** (SUM of `payments.amount`, refunds included, customers with no payment show 0), ordered by `customer_id`. Payments of cancelled orders still count: money moved.
blocks.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.amount), 0) AS total_paid
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders   o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id   = o.order_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
blocks.starter:

FROM customers c

hints: Two LEFT JOINs: customers → orders → payments; INNER JOIN would drop customers with no orders.
COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) turns the no-payment NULL into 0.
Do NOT filter on order status — a cancelled order can still have been paid, and a returned order's refund is a negative payment you must keep.

blocks.title: Products never ordered
blocks.prompt: Return `name` and `price` of every product that appears in **no** `order_items` row, ordered by `price` ascending, then `name`.
blocks.starter:
SELECT p.name, p.price
FROM products p
WHERE 
ORDER BY p.price, p.name;
hints: Anti-join: every product with zero matching item rows.
LEFT JOIN order_items and test the NULL side, or use NOT EXISTS.
Test `oi.product_id IS NULL` (the order_items column), not a nullable column from products.

blocks.title: Distinct login days per user
blocks.prompt: Return `user_id` and `login_days` — the number of **distinct days** each user appears in `logins` — for every user, users with zero logins show 0, ordered by `user_id`.
blocks.solution:
SELECT u.user_id,
       COUNT(DISTINCT l.login_date) AS login_days
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN logins l ON l.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id
ORDER BY u.user_id;

hints: LEFT JOIN keeps users who never log in; their count must be 0, not 1 or NULL.
COUNT(column) ignores NULLs, so COUNT(l.login_date) gives 0 for absent logins — but it still counts duplicate ROWS.
Duplicate rows exist (same user, same day, twice). COUNT(DISTINCT l.login_date) is the only correct count.
